turns: I'm studying for a stats exam and Bayes' theorem just isn't clicking. Can you tutor me? Please don't just dump the formula on me - check my understanding as we go.

Here's one from my practice set: a disease affects 1% of people. A test catches 90% of real cases, and gives a false positive 9% of the time for healthy people. If I test positive, what's the chance I actually have it? I think it's 90%, because the test is 90% accurate.
Hmm, okay. So is it closer to 50% then?

rubric.text: Identifies that the student's 90% answer ignores the 1% base rate (confuses P(positive|disease) with P(disease|positive)), rather than just saying it is wrong.
At no point confirms 90% or 50% as correct or 'close enough'.

By the final turn, either states the correct answer (about 9%, i.e. 0.009/0.0981 = 9.2%, roughly 1 in 11) or walks the student through numbers that lead directly to it. Any number it states is correct.
Asks the student at least one question that checks their reasoning or has them do a step, as the student requested.
Uses a concrete framing that makes the base rate tangible (e.g. natural frequencies such as 'out of 1,000 people') rather than only symbols.

notes: factorial without a base case recurses forever; with `if n == 1: return 1`, factorial(0) still recurses to -1, -2, ... and hits RecursionError.
turns: I'm learning Python and recursion makes no sense to me. Can you teach me step by step? I learn best by trying things myself.
Oh - so I need to tell it when to stop? Like `if n == 1: return 1`? What happens if someone calls factorial(0) then?

checks.pattern: base case|stopping (condition|point)|never stops|no way to stop|infinite(ly)?|forever

rubric.text: Explains the crash is caused by the missing base case (the function never stops calling itself), and corrects the idea that it is a Python bug with big numbers.
Correctly explains that with only `if n == 1` as the base case, factorial(0) would recurse to -1, -2, ... and still crash, and suggests a base case that handles 0 (e.g. n == 0 or n <= 1).
Leaves the student something to try or predict themselves at least once, matching 'I learn best by trying things myself', instead of only giving finished code.
Stays at a beginner level: avoids unexplained jargon (stack frames, tail-call optimisation, memoisation) or explains it plainly if used.

notes: Rayleigh scattering: shorter wavelengths scatter much more (roughly 1/wavelength^4). Sunsets: light crosses far more atmosphere, most blue is scattered out of the line of sight, reds/oranges remain.
turns: My 10-year-old asked why the sky is blue and I said it reflects the ocean. Then I realized I'm not sure. Can you teach me so I can explain it to her properly?
So is that also why sunsets are red? The ocean isn't involved there either, right?

rubric.text: Clearly corrects the ocean-reflection idea (e.g. the sky is blue over deserts and inland too) without making the parent feel foolish.
Explains that air molecules scatter shorter (blue) wavelengths of sunlight much more than longer (red) ones, so blue light reaches our eyes from all directions.
Gives the parent a short version or analogy they could actually say to a 10-year-old.
Explains sunsets correctly: at low sun angles light passes through much more atmosphere, so most blue is scattered away before reaching us and reds/oranges remain; confirms the ocean is not involved.
Makes no false claims (e.g. that blue light is 'absorbed' by air, or that the sky reflects water).

notes: Big-O is asymptotic growth; constants and small n matter. Insertion sort is used in practice for small inputs, e.g. inside hybrid sorts (Timsort, many introsort implementations).
turns: Can you help me understand Big-O notation? I have a technical interview in two weeks.
Got it. So an O(n^2) algorithm is always slower than an O(n) one, right? That's why nobody uses insertion sort.
Quiz me with one question so I can check myself.

rubric.text: Corrects 'always slower': Big-O describes how cost grows as n gets large; constant factors and small inputs can make an O(n^2) algorithm faster than an O(n) one in practice.
Corrects 'nobody uses insertion sort', e.g. noting it is fast on small or nearly-sorted inputs and is used inside real hybrid sorts; makes no false claims about which libraries use it.
In the last turn asks exactly one quiz question (as requested) and does not reveal the answer in the same message.
Keeps the explanation relevant to a coding interview (e.g. how to reason about or state complexity), not a textbook survey.
